sections.text: Extended Follow-up of Type 1 Diabetes Immunotherapy Trial Participants Suggests Benign Side Effect Profile
OBJECTIVE
Long-term side effect surveillance after immunotherapy clinical trial participation in individuals with or at risk of type 1 diabetes is needed.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS

Participants from 14 randomized controlled trials (47%) joined the Long-term Investigative Follow-up in Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet or Immune Tolerance Network Type 1 Diabetes Extension Study, and 98% answered at least one health-related outcomes question.
RESULTS

Participants were observed for a median of 1.78 (interquartile range 0.89–4.04) years after original trial completion and, in some, up to 18 years. There were no differences in the frequency of self-reported health outcomes, including moderate to severe hypoglycemia events, hospitalizations, serious infections (including COVID-19 infection), new allergic reactions, autoimmune disease, and cancer incidence, between those receiving active and placebo therapy (n = 209–473 responses per question; P > 0.05 for all).
CONCLUSIONS

We observed no differences in self-reported health outcomes between those who received active immunotherapy versus placebo. Continued long-term follow-up of immunotherapy trial participants is essential.
Graphical Abstract
Introduction

Immune-based therapies are classically used to induce significant immune suppression to bring about disease amelioration or resolution (e.g., prevention of transplant rejection). However, significant adverse effects can occur, such as serious infections, bone marrow suppression, and other organ-specific toxicities. The goal of disease-modifying immunotherapy in the management and/or prevention of type 1 diabetes is not immune suppression but rather immune modulation and β-cell preservation. Early immune therapy trials in type 1 diabetes had unacceptably high rates of significant adverse effects (e.g., renal toxicity associated with cyclosporine as well as azathioprine plus prednisone treatment). More recently, lower rates of adverse events in trials using more targeted immunotherapies have been observed; however, data from long-term follow--up of these participants are unavailable.

We assessed adverse effects beyond the time of the original immunotherapy trials in the Long-term Investigative Follow-up in TrialNet study (TN16 LIFT) by Type 1 Diabetes TrialNet through 31 January 2025 and the Type 1 Diabetes Extension Study (ITN066AI T1DES; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02734277) by Immune Tolerance Network (ITN) through 20 February 2025.
Research Design and Methods

Placebo- and drug-treated participants from 14 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) by TrialNet and ITN were offered enrollment, after the conclusion of the original trials, into long-term monitoring protocols. TrialNet participants with stage 3 disease were offered enrollment in LIFT directly after completion of the original RCTs (n = 627). TrialNet participants in prevention trials whose disease had not progressed to stage 3 were observed in a separate protocol (TN01 Pathway to Prevention study; n = 242) and received similar health-related questionnaires. Both groups of TrialNet participants were combined as LIFT participants for the purposes of this analysis. ITN trial participants were offered participation in T1DES after their parent study ended: 0.4 years after Tocilizumab (TCZ) in New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes (EXTEND) trial (n = 63), 3 years after the Inducing Remission in New-Onset Type 1 Diabetes With Alefacept (T1DAL) trial (n = 12), and 7 years after the Autoimmunity-Blocking Antibody for Tolerance in Recently Diagnosed Type 1 Diabetes (AbATE) trial (n = 14). TrialNet trials according to disease stage were as follows: stage 1 (multiple islet autoantibodies with normoglycemia): TN07 trial of insulin antigen therapy with median follow-up of 2.7 (inquartile range [IQR] 1.5–4.7) years during treatment, TN18 trial of abatacept with 1–8 years of follow-up (1-year treatment), and TN22 trial of hydroxychloroquine (terminated because of futility); stage 1/2: TN20 trial of insulin antigen therapy with 1 year of follow-up (6-month treatment; ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT02580877); stage 2 (multiple autoantibodies with dysglycemia): TN10 trial of teplizumab with 74 days to 7.6 years of follow-up (14-day treatment); and stage 3: TN05 trial of rituximab with 2 years of follow-up (1-month treatment), TN08 trial of glutamic acid decarboxylase antigen therapy with 1 year of follow-up (two to three doses of treatment), TN09 trial of abatacept with 3 years of follow-up (2-year treatment), TN14 trial of canakinumab with 1 year of treatment/follow-up, TN19 trial of ATG with or without granulocyte colony-stimulating factor with 2 years of follow-up (2-day treatment with ATG ± 10 weeks of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor), and TN27 trial of NNC0361-0041 antigen therapy with 1 year of follow-up (12-week treatment). All ITN trials were conducted in patients with stage 3 type 1 diabetes: EXTEND trial of tocilizumab with 2 years of follow-up (6-month treatment), T1DAL trial of alefacept with 2 years of follow-up (two 3-month treatments), and AbATE trial of hOKT3gamma1 teplizumab with 2 years of follow-up (two 14-day treatments).

Participants from LIFT (n = 869) and T1DES (n = 89) databases who had at least one visit were included. Follow-up typically occurred at 6-month intervals but was variable. Actively treated and placebo-treated participants were compared for each health-related outcome. In LIFT, a health questionnaire was filled out on paper or via phone by the participant or parent/caregiver (Supplementary Material Appendix A), and in T1DES, protocol-specific adverse events were queried at each visit (Supplementary Material Appendix B). When survey questions overlapped between LIFT and T1DES, the data were combined. Hypoglycemia was defined in LIFT as “ever reported any moderate hypoglycemia episodes where you might have been confused, disoriented, or lethargic and were unable to treat yourself.” Hypoglycemia was defined in T1DES as glucose concentration <55 mg/dL (3 mmol/L; by glucometer or continuous glucose monitor) or clinically as hypoglycemia involving seizure or loss of consciousness or requiring external assistance to recover. The frequencies of participants ever experiencing each outcome were compared between treatment arms using the χ2 or Fisher exact test if an individual sample size was fewer than five. Numeric parameters, such as length of follow-up, were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test. P values <0.05 were considered significant. All statistical testing was performed using SAS version 9.4 (Cary, NC).
Results

From 14 RCTs, 47% (958 of 2,020) of participants entered long-term monitoring, and of those, 98% (938 of 958) answered at least one health-related question, but only up to 49% (n = 473 of 958) of participants answered the same question. Among all participants (N = 958), the median (IQR) age at initial follow-up was 15 (11–21) years, and 59.6% were male, 92.1% identified as White, and 91.3% identified as non-Hispanic/Latino. The median (IQR) time participants were observed in TrialNet LIFT or ITN T1DES was 1.81 (0.97–4.12) years in 644 participants treated with active therapy and 1.74 (0.65–3.53) years in 314 participants treated with placebo (P = 0.127). Total time elapsed since active therapy or placebo administration ranged from ∼0.5 to 15 years in LIFT and ∼3.5 to 18 years in T1DES.

There was no difference between actively treated and placebo-treated individuals in the frequency of moderate or severe hypoglycemia episodes. Additionally, there were no differences in hospitalizations, any opportunistic or serious infections, COVID-19 infection (tabulated beginning in 2020), new allergic reactions, new autoimmune diseases, or new cancer diagnoses between actively treated and placebo-treated individuals (Fig. 1). Number of respondents per question, median follow-up time, and statistical differences are shown in Fig. 1. Of note, 56 individuals from the TN10 trial (33 receiving teplizumab 23 receiving placebo) were observed for a median (IQR) of 3.69 (1.61–5.45) years, and their results mirror those of the entire cohort.

TrialNet LIFT adult participants were asked if they had “ever reported problems conceiving a child,” to which 1.0% (2 of 205) in the active therapy arm and 1.8% (2 of 114) in the placebo arm answered positively (P = 0.549). Of respondents, 2.9% (6 of 205) and 1.8% (2 of 114) in the active and placebo arms, respectively, had gotten a partner pregnant (P = 0.521). No one (0 of 205) in the active therapy arm and 1.8% (2 of 114) in the placebo arm had “ever reported a miscarriage” (P = 0.127); 0.5% (1 of 205) and 0.9% (1 of 114), respectively, had “ever reported a stillbirth” (P = 0.673). No one reported having a child with birth defects.

Since completion of the parent study, 7 of 143 respondents (4.9%) from an active therapy arm reported experiencing diabetes-related ketoacidosis (DKA) (four in LIFT and three in T1DES), and zero of 66 from the placebo arm reported DKA (P = 0.100). Of note, one individual in T1DES reported six episodes of DKA.

Participants were also queried if they had “ever reported acute coronary syndrome” (LIFT) or “cardiovascular disease (including myocardial infarction/acute coronary syndrome, stroke, or transient ischemic attack)” (T1DES), and no participants answered in the affirmative in either treatment arm. Two deaths occurred during follow-up in ITN T1DES: 1) from pneumonia 20.9 months after the last dose of tocilizumab (determined unlikely related) and 2) from a motor vehicle collision 58.9 months after placebo (unrelated).

Of note, 12 individuals who received active therapy (i.e., teplizumab) in the ITN AbATE trial were observed for a median (IQR) of 10.07 (8.07–15.49) years. Compared with the two concurrent control group individuals who experienced zero events (observed for a median [IQR] of 12.76 [7.67–17.85] years), the participants receiving active therapy experienced one episode of hypoglycemia (P = 0.672), two hospitalizations (P = 0.533), and one opportunistic or serious infection (P = 0.672). Neither the control nor active therapy arms reported any episodes of DKA, acute coronary syndrome, malignancy, pregnancy, new autoimmune disease, or new hypersensitivity to unrelated allergens.

One ITN T1DAL participant who received alefacept had two pregnancies, 3 and 5 years after study completion. In the first pregnancy, the participant delivered 5 weeks early, and the infant required hospitalization for 20 days because of pulmonary issues and hypoglycemia. In the second pregnancy, the participant had an uncomplicated term delivery. No congenital anomalies were reported.

Finally, participants receiving therapies with transient depletion in lymphocyte counts were combined across networks and compared against their placebo-treated counterparts. These therapies included rituximab (TN05), teplizumab (TN10 and AbATE), canakinumab (TN14), low-dose ATG (TN19), and tocilizumab (EXTEND). There were no differences in hypoglycemia, DKA, hospitalizations, COVID-19 or other infections, new allergic reactions, autoimmune disease, or cancer diagnoses between those treated with active therapy and those receiving placebo (Supplementary Table 1). There were similar outcomes when combining those therapies without direct effects on lymphocyte counts (insulin antigen therapy [TN07, TN20, and TN27], GAD antigen therapy [TN08], abatacept [TN09 and TN18], alefacept [T1DAL], and hydroxychloroquine [TN22]) as well as when combining TN10 and AbATE data to compare teplizumab-treated participants with participants receiving placebo (Supplementary Table 1).
Conclusions

This study represents the largest long-term follow-up of individuals at various stages of type 1 diabetes who received immunotherapy in a clinical trial. Immunotherapy adverse effects experienced during the included trials were mostly therapy specific. Of note, several of these immunotherapies produce transient lymphodepletion (e.g., teplizumab, ATG, and rituximab), and none was associated with an increased rate of infection, opportunistic infection, or COVID-19 infection during longer-term posttrial follow-up. A small number of DKA events occurred in the active therapy arms, whereas none occurred in the placebo arms. This difference was not statistically significant and requires corroboration in larger samples.

Our combined data set represents 958 of 2,020 possible participants (47%), of whom 938 answered a health-related survey question (98%), with up to 473 answering the same question. An additional limitation is that these long-term follow-up protocols included individuals who 1) chose to enter an RCT and 2) chose to continue in a different long-term research protocol. This selection bias may limit the generalizability of these findings, because those who enroll in clinical trials are not representative of the entire population with the disease.

In summary, we observed no difference in self-reported health outcomes between trial participants who received active therapy and those who received placebo, suggesting the benign nature, from an adverse effects standpoint, of these therapies long term. However, longer-term follow-up, especially among older individuals, is warranted. Before joining a trial or recommending a new therapy, both families and clinicians often want to know if there are long-term consequences or safety issues. These data may inform the risk/benefit ratio for future trials, permitting adequate informed consent. Such long-term follow-up is vital as we move toward regulatory approval of additional disease-modifying therapies in type 1 diabetes.
